solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Weirdo Sid Owen tackles a bit of a dance (4-2)

indicatorNotes.tackles: to tackle is to grip, so the phrase holds the answer's letters

blocks.note: weirDO SID Owen: the answer runs across the word breaks

annotation.surface: An odd character called Sid Owen is attempting a dance step.
annotation.walkthrough: Sid Owen is a real actor, so the name reads as the subject; it is only the container for the letters. 'Tackles' looks like football, not a hidden-word signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A do-si-do is a figure in square dancing where partners circle back to back, so it is one bit of a dance.

entries.clue: Stop son being adopted by believer in God (6)

indicatorNotes.being adopted by: something adopted is taken in, so S goes inside the believer

blocks.note: a deist believes in God without revealed religion

annotation.surface: A son is taken in by a devout family, and someone wants it stopped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Adopted' paints a family scene; it is the container signal, taking S into the believer. A deist believes in a creator God but not in revelation.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to desist is to cease, used of an action one is told to give up.

entries.clue: Cry before party managed to clear one’s head (7,2)

annotation.surface: Someone weeps before a party and somehow gets their thoughts straight.
annotation.walkthrough: The DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland. The picture of tears before a party hides a morning-after answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Having sobered up, one's head is clear again after drinking.

entries.clue: Band member Joe famously losing stone for daughter (7)

indicatorNotes.losing: to lose something is to go without it, so ST drops out of the name
indicatorNotes.for: 'for' in the sense of 'in exchange for': D is swapped in where ST was

blocks.note: Joe STRUMMER without ST (stone, the weight)

annotation.surface: A famous rocker called Joe is dropping weight, apparently for his daughter's sake.
annotation.walkthrough: Joe Strummer was the singer of The Clash, so 'Band member' feels like it belongs to the wordplay. ST is the standard abbreviation for stone, the 14-pound weight.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by role: the drummer keeps the beat in a band, and the surface's rock star makes it apt.

entries.clue: Cold Bud also served – a gassy drink lacking flavour (4,4)

indicatorNotes.served: the letters are dished up in a new arrangement

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on a tap

annotation.surface: A bar order: a cold Budweiser, plus something fizzy and bland.
annotation.walkthrough: Bud is Budweiser beer, which makes the whole thing read as a drinks order; the brand name is just letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Club soda is carbonated water, fizzy and without flavour.

entries.clue: Is it Victor’s round? (3,2,6)

blocks.note: read as a man called Victor, and meant as the victor, whoever has just won
read as his turn to buy the drinks, and meant as a circuit of the track

annotation.surface: Someone in a pub asks whether it is Victor's turn to buy the drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital V hides the plain word victor, and the pub setting makes 'round' a round of drinks rather than a lap.
annotation.definitionFit: A lap of honour is the celebratory circuit a race winner runs, so it is literally the victor's round.

entries.clue: Swaggering display from Charlie’s predecessor screening commercial (7)

indicatorNotes.screening: to screen is to hide behind, so BRAVO surrounds AD

blocks.note: in the NATO alphabet Alpha, Bravo, Charlie: Bravo comes before Charlie

annotation.surface: A showy performance from the man who had Charlie's job before, blocking an advert.
annotation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a person with a predecessor in office; it is a letter of the radio alphabet, and the one before it is Bravo.
annotation.definitionFit: Bravado is a bold, swaggering show of confidence.

entries.clue: Due over £1000 after securing victory (5)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' in its sense of 'following': G is written following O
indicatorNotes.securing: to secure is to hold fast, so O and G hold WIN between them

blocks.note: O = over, as on a cricket scorecard

annotation.surface: A payment of over a thousand pounds falls due after someone wins.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'more than' the sum; it is simply O. A grand is slang for £1000.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: money that is due is still owing to someone.

entries.clue: Lawyer dined outside, in two minds over starter of yakitori (8)

indicatorNotes.outside: ATE is placed on the outside, wrapping round TORN
indicatorNotes.starter of: a starter is what comes first, so take the first letter

annotation.surface: A lawyer eats outdoors, dithering over a skewer of Japanese chicken for a starter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dined outside' paints eating al fresco; 'outside' is the container signal. Yakitori is Japanese grilled chicken on skewers.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym with a regional lean: attorney is the usual American word for a lawyer.

entries.clue: Quiet vehicle on the way back departs Uxbridge empty (6)

indicatorNotes.on the way back: a vehicle on its way back is going in reverse, so BUS reads backwards
indicatorNotes.empty: an empty word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer letters

annotation.surface: A quiet bus on its return journey leaves Uxbridge with no passengers.
annotation.walkthrough: Uxbridge is a town on the western edge of London, which suits the bus picture. 'Quiet' is a verb here, not an adjective describing the bus.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as verbs: to quiet a rowdy crowd is to subdue it.

entries.clue: One likely to experience a buzz at work? (8)

annotation.definition: One likely to experience a buzz at work?

blocks.note: read as feeling a thrill, and meant as hearing bees hum
the job itself is where the humming happens: tending hives

annotation.surface: Someone who gets a thrill from their job.
annotation.walkthrough: A buzz reads as excitement; for a beekeeper it is the noise of the hives.
annotation.definitionFit: An apiarist keeps bees, so their working day is spent amid buzzing.

entries.clue: Specialist at Rugby School initially caught harmful flies (5,4)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letter of School
indicatorNotes.flies: the letters fly about into a new order

blocks.note: C = caught, on a cricket scorecard

annotation.surface: At Rugby School, someone has caught dangerous insects.
annotation.walkthrough: Rugby School is a famous English boarding school, and the capital S makes it one phrase; split it so 'Rugby' goes with the definition and 'School' with the wordplay. 'Flies' looks like insects.
annotation.definitionFit: The scrum half is a specialist rugby position, feeding the ball into the scrum.

entries.clue: Each April, go around the Aegean (11)

annotation.definitionNote: a definition by example: the Aegean islands are the original archipelago
annotation.surface: An invitation to tour the Greek islands every spring.
annotation.walkthrough: The word archipelago was first the name of the Aegean Sea itself, with its scattering of islands, so the definition is historically exact.
annotation.definitionFit: The Aegean, dotted with islands, is the original archipelago.

entries.clue: Carnegie regularly displayed onset of real temper (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly displayed: what is displayed at regular intervals is every other letter
indicatorNotes.onset of: the onset of something is its beginning, so take the first letter

annotation.surface: Andrew Carnegie routinely showed the first signs of a genuine temper.
annotation.walkthrough: Andrew Carnegie was the steel magnate, a plausible subject for a temper; his name here only supplies alternate letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: temper in the sense of a fit of rage, as in 'lose one's temper'.

entries.clue: Cathedral cook toyed with a bit of Black Magic (4,9)

indicatorNotes.toyed with: the letters are played with into a new order

annotation.surface: A cook at a cathedral dabbled in the occult.
annotation.walkthrough: Black Magic is a British box of dark chocolates; the capitals are the only hint that it is a brand, not sorcery.
annotation.definitionFit: Each piece in a box of Black Magic is a dark chocolate.

entries.clue: Like a tumbler going from bar to bar? (9)

annotation.definition: Like a tumbler going from bar to bar?

blocks.note: read as a drinking glass, and meant as a gymnast who tumbles
read as a pub crawl, and meant as swinging between trapeze bars

annotation.surface: A glass being passed along from pub to pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinking reading of both 'tumbler' and 'bar' is so natural that the circus reading is easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A tumbler flying from bar to bar is performing acrobatics.

entries.clue: Fuel smell upset airborne soldier at the front (8)

indicatorNotes.upset: to upset is to knock over, and in a down clue NIFF is turned upside down
indicatorNotes.at the front: the soldier stands at the front, so PARA comes first

blocks.note: niff is British slang for a bad smell

annotation.surface: A whiff of fuel bothers the paratrooper leading the way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the soldier being bothered by the smell; it is the turnaround signal. Niff is British slang for a stink.
annotation.definitionFit: Paraffin is a fuel, what Americans call kerosene.

entries.clue: Whisk a red pepper with oil for the perfect look (5-3,5)

annotation.surface: A cooking tip: blend red pepper with oil to make a dish look just right.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen surface makes 'Whisk' an instruction to the cook. Apple-pie order has nothing to do with pie: it means everything neat.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: apple-pie order means perfect neatness, so a room in it has the perfect look.

entries.clue: Overshadow cuts in electronic energy (7)

indicatorNotes.in: CLIPS goes inside the two Es

annotation.surface: A blackout of electrical power casts a shadow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cuts in electronic energy' reads as power cuts; 'cuts' is a verb and 'in' the container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym by metaphor: one body eclipsing another blocks its light, just as a rival overshadows.

entries.clue: Desperate character rues playing a bloke in tights (7)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters of RUES perform in a new arrangement

blocks.note: Desperate Dan, the cowboy strongman of the British comic The Dandy

annotation.surface: A man in despair regrets taking on the role of someone in tights.
annotation.walkthrough: Desperate Dan is the pie-eating giant of the British children's comic The Dandy, so 'Desperate character' is a named figure, not a mood.
annotation.definitionFit: A danseur is a male ballet dancer, and ballet men dance in tights.

entries.clue: Stuck in Agadir by hotel, flipping cross (6)

indicatorNotes.Stuck in: the answer is lodged inside the phrase
indicatorNotes.flipping: the letters are turned the other way

annotation.surface: Someone stranded in Agadir next to their hotel is furious.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild curse, flipping cross meaning very angry; it is the reversal signal, and 'cross' is a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A hybrid is a cross between two breeds or varieties.

entries.clue: Associated Press: China Shock (5)

blocks.note: china plate = mate in Cockney rhyming slang, and a mate is a pal

annotation.surface: A news-agency headline about a shock in China.
annotation.walkthrough: China is the country in the headline; in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, shortened to china.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as verbs: to appal is to horrify or shock.

entries.clue: Vertical chimney oil company put up outside (5)

indicatorNotes.put up: to put up is to raise, and in a down clue raising BP reverses it
indicatorNotes.outside: PB is placed on the outside of LUM

blocks.note: lum is the Scots word for a chimney

annotation.surface: An oil company erects a tall chimney outdoors.
annotation.walkthrough: Lum is Scots for chimney, a crossword regular; 'put up' sounds like building, but it flips BP upward.
annotation.definitionFit: Plumb means exactly vertical, as a plumb line hangs.

entries.clue: He’s sent to fetch injured Red Baron back from Blighty (6,3)

indicatorNotes.injured: injured letters are damaged out of shape, so rearrange them
indicatorNotes.back from: the back of a word is its end, so take the last letter

annotation.surface: An airman is sent to bring the wounded Red Baron home from Britain.
annotation.walkthrough: The Red Baron was the German First World War flying ace, and Blighty is old soldiers' slang for Britain, so the surface is a wartime story. 'Back from' means the last letter, not a return trip.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by role: fetching and carrying is exactly the errand boy's job.

entries.clue: Murder of rejected university student drama (4,4)

indicatorNotes.rejected: turned back, so OF becomes FO

annotation.surface: A student play about a murder was turned down by the university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rejected university student' reads as one unlucky applicant; 'rejected' only turns back the little word 'of'.
annotation.definitionFit: Police suspecting foul play suspect murder.

entries.clue: Metal safe storing whiskey (6)

indicatorNotes.storing: the safe holds W inside it

blocks.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

annotation.surface: A metal safe with a bottle of whiskey locked inside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Metal safe' reads as one object; 'Metal' is the definition, and peter is safecrackers' slang for a safe.
annotation.definitionFit: Pewter is a tin-based metal alloy.

entries.clue: Swiss bar closing early to switch walls, getting a kind of mould (5,3)

indicatorNotes.closing early: the word stops before its last letter

blocks.note: TOBLERONE, the Swiss chocolate bar, minus its last letter
the outer letters T and N swap places

annotation.surface: A Swiss bar shuts early to change its décor, and mould turns up.
annotation.walkthrough: The Swiss bar is Toblerone, the triangular chocolate, not a place to drink; its 'walls' are its first and last letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Noble rot is the grey mould Botrytis, prized for shrivelling grapes into sweet wine.

entries.clue: Ready for attack, Pitt taking on both Conservative wings (6)

indicatorNotes.taking on: to take on is to take in, so BRAD takes CE inside it
indicatorNotes.both: both wings, left and right, not just one
indicatorNotes.wings: a word's wings are its outer letters, as a party's wings are its extremes

annotation.surface: Prime Minister Pitt takes on both factions of the Tory party.
annotation.walkthrough: Pitt with Conservative reads as William Pitt, the Tory Prime Minister; it is Brad Pitt the film star.
annotation.definitionFit: Braced means prepared for an impact or attack.
